questions.topic: Ch 13 · Scheme · Nature of the Act
questions.stem: The General Clauses Act 1897 is best described as:
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897 — scheme and object

readLink.label: Read: Purpose and scheme of the Act →

options.text: A statute about statutes — a dictionary of expressions and a body of default rules of construction which apply to Central Acts and Regulations unless the context otherwise requires
options.explanation: Correct. The Act creates almost no substantive rights. It defines expressions once (s. 3), supplies defaults where a later Act is silent (ss. 5, 6, 9, 14), and guards against drafting slips (ss. 6, 24) — all subject to a contrary intention or a repugnant context.

options.text: A code of substantive rights which overrides every Central Act with which it conflicts
options.explanation: It creates no code of substantive rights, and it does not override. Nearly every operative provision yields where the later enactment shows a different intention or the subject or context is repugnant.

options.text: A procedural code governing the conduct of proceedings before courts and tribunals
options.explanation: Procedure before courts is governed by the Codes of Civil and Criminal Procedure. Section 10 touches a court's closed days, but that is a rule of computation, not a code of procedure.

options.text: A statute which applies uniformly to Central Acts and to the Acts of every State legislature
options.explanation: It reads CENTRAL Acts and Regulations. Each State has enacted its own General Clauses Act for its own legislation.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · Scheme · Application of the Act
questions.stem: The General Clauses Act 1897 applies to:
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, ss. 3, 4 and 4A — application

readLink.label: Read: Purpose and scheme of the Act →

options.text: Every Act in force in India, whether made by Parliament or by a State legislature
options.explanation: State legislation is read by the State's own General Clauses Act. The 1897 Act does not supply the defaults for a State Act.

options.text: Central Acts passed after the Constitution came into force, and to nothing earlier
options.explanation: The Act long predates the Constitution and its principal definitions are carried back to Central Acts made after 1868. There is no post-Constitution cut-off.

options.text: Central Acts and Regulations, and the rules, regulations and bye-laws made under Central Acts
options.explanation: Correct. The Act reads Central legislation and what hangs off it — the s. 3 definitions are applied to Central Acts and Regulations and, through the extending provisions, to subordinate legislation made under them.

options.text: Regulations only, the expression 'Act' being expressly excluded from its operation
options.explanation: The reverse of the truth: 'enactment' in this Act expressly includes a Regulation, and the Act plainly applies to Central Acts.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · Scheme · When the Act does not apply
questions.stem: A Central Act passed in 2026 defines 'document' for its own purposes in terms narrower than the definition in section 3 of the General Clauses Act 1897. In construing the 2026 Act, the definition to be applied is:
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 3 — 'unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context'

readLink.label: Read: Purpose and scheme of the Act →

options.text: The General Clauses Act definition, because a general Act of Parliament of 1897 cannot be displaced by a later Act which does not repeal it
options.explanation: The 1897 definitions are defaults, not overriding provisions. A later Act displaces them simply by defining the expression for itself.

options.text: Whichever of the two definitions produces the result more favourable to the person affected
options.explanation: There is no such rule of selection. The special definition governs regardless of whom it favours.

options.text: Both definitions cumulatively, so that a matter falling within either is a 'document'
options.explanation: Cumulation is exactly what the opening words of s. 3 prevent. Where the enactment supplies its own meaning, the general definition steps aside altogether.

options.text: The narrower definition in the 2026 Act, because the section 3 definitions apply only where there is nothing repugnant in the subject or context and the enactment does not supply its own meaning
options.explanation: Correct. Section 3 opens with the qualification 'unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context'. A definition written into the enactment being construed is the plainest possible contrary indication.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Affidavit
questions.stem: Under section 3 of the General Clauses Act 1897, the expression 'affidavit':

readLink.label: Read: Section 3 — the definitions that matter →

options.text: Means only a statement sworn on oath before a person authorised to administer oaths, and nothing else
options.explanation: That is the ordinary meaning, which the definition deliberately extends. The definition uses 'shall include', not 'shall mean'.

options.text: Includes affirmation and declaration in the case of persons by law allowed to affirm or declare instead of swearing
options.explanation: Correct. The extension is limited to that class — persons whom the law permits to affirm or declare in place of swearing. For them an affirmation or declaration is an affidavit.

options.text: Includes any signed written statement, whether or not it is sworn, affirmed or declared
options.explanation: Far too wide. An unsworn, unaffirmed written statement is not an affidavit merely because it is signed.

options.text: Includes an oral statement recorded by a court in the course of a proceeding
options.explanation: Deposition on oath in court is not an affidavit. The definition extends the mode of verification, not the medium.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Act and illegal omission
questions.stem: Section 3 of the General Clauses Act 1897 provides that the word 'act', used with reference to an offence or a civil wrong:

readLink.label: Read: Section 3 — the definitions that matter →

options.text: Includes a series of acts, and words which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs matter: a course of conduct is caught as an 'act', and words about acts done reach omissions — but only omissions which are ILLEGAL, and in the offence or civil-wrong context in which the definition is expressed to operate.

options.text: Includes every omission, whether legal or illegal, in every context in which the word is used
options.explanation: Two errors. The omission must be illegal, and the definition is expressed to operate with reference to an offence or a civil wrong, not at large.

options.text: Is confined to a single completed act and cannot be read to cover a course of conduct
options.explanation: The definition says the opposite — it expressly includes a series of acts, so a continuing course of conduct is caught.

options.text: Includes a series of acts but can never be extended to cover any omission
options.explanation: Half right and therefore wrong: the definition expressly extends words referring to acts done to illegal omissions.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Document
questions.stem: Which of the following best states the definition of 'document' in section 3 of the General Clauses Act 1897?

readLink.label: Read: Section 3 — the definitions that matter →

options.text: Only a writing on paper signed by the person making it
options.explanation: Neither paper nor signature appears in the definition. Any substance and any of the listed means will do.

options.text: Only matter recorded in electronic form, the earlier definition having been superseded
options.explanation: Nothing has superseded the definition. Electronic records are dealt with by separate legislation; the General Clauses Act definition remains as it stands and is medium-neutral.

options.text: Any matter written, expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks, or by more than one of those means, which is intended to be used, or which may be used, for the purpose of recording that matter
options.explanation: Correct. Three elements: matter expressed on any SUBSTANCE, by letters, figures or marks (or a combination), with the purpose or capacity of RECORDING that matter.

options.text: Any matter recorded on any substance, provided the record has been registered under the law relating to the registration of documents
options.explanation: Registration is a separate concept, defined elsewhere in s. 3. An unregistered writing is still a document.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Good faith
questions.stem: A thing is deemed to be done in 'good faith' within the meaning of the General Clauses Act 1897 where it is:

readLink.label: Read: Good faith, person and property →

options.text: Done with due care and attention, negligence being inconsistent with good faith
options.explanation: That is the standard imported by section 52 of the Indian Penal Code, which reverses the General Clauses Act test. It is the single most common wrong answer in this chapter.

options.text: Done honestly and in the belief that it is lawful, provided reasonable enquiry has first been made
options.explanation: The enquiry requirement is invented. The definition asks only whether the thing was in fact done honestly.

options.text: Done in the honest belief that it will benefit the person affected by it
options.explanation: Benefit to the person affected is irrelevant. Honesty of the doer is the whole of the test.

options.text: In fact done honestly, whether it is done negligently or not
options.explanation: Correct. The General Clauses Act test is subjective honesty, and negligence is expressly declared immaterial.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Good faith contrasted with the IPC
questions.stem: Roshan, a clerk, despatches a statutory notice to an address which he honestly believes to be current but which he would have found to be stale had he consulted the register kept beside him. Which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 3 ('good faith'); Indian Penal Code, s. 52

readLink.label: Read: Good faith, person and property →

options.text: He acts in good faith both under the General Clauses Act and under the Indian Penal Code, honesty being the test under each
options.explanation: The Penal Code test is not honesty. Section 52 of the IPC excludes anything done without due care and attention.

options.text: He acts in good faith under the General Clauses Act, where honesty suffices, but not under the Indian Penal Code, section 52 of which excludes anything done without due care and attention
options.explanation: Correct. The same conduct can be in good faith under one statute and outside it under the other. Where an enactment supplies its own definition it governs; where it does not, the General Clauses Act honesty test carries over.

options.text: He acts in good faith under neither, negligence defeating good faith under both statutes
options.explanation: Under the General Clauses Act negligence is expressly immaterial — a thing is in good faith if in fact done honestly, 'whether it is done negligently or not'.

options.text: He acts in good faith under the Indian Penal Code but not under the General Clauses Act
options.explanation: This inverts both definitions. The IPC is the stricter of the two, not the laxer.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Immovable property
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT immovable property as defined by section 3 of the General Clauses Act 1897?

readLink.label: Read: Section 3 — the definitions that matter →

options.text: A portable diesel generator resting on a factory floor by its own weight and not attached to the earth
options.explanation: Correct. It is neither land, nor a benefit arising out of land, nor a thing attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything so attached. Failing all three limbs, it falls into the residual definition of movable property.

options.text: Land
options.explanation: Land is the first limb of the definition.

options.text: A right to collect tolls at a private bridge
options.explanation: A right to collect tolls is a benefit to arise out of land, which the definition expressly includes.

options.text: An overhead water tank permanently fastened to a concrete plinth cast into the ground
options.explanation: A thing permanently fastened to something attached to the earth — squarely within the third limb.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Movable property
questions.stem: 'Movable property' is defined by the General Clauses Act 1897 as:

readLink.label: Read: Section 3 — the definitions that matter →

options.text: Goods and merchandise only, actionable claims and other intangible property being excluded
options.explanation: No such exclusion appears. The definition is residual and sweeps in every description of property that is not immovable.

options.text: Every kind of property which is in fact capable of being physically moved from one place to another
options.explanation: Physical portability is not the test. A right or a claim cannot be carried anywhere, yet it is movable property because it is not immovable.

options.text: Property of every description except immovable property
options.explanation: Correct. The definition is residual, which is why the working method is to test immovability first — whatever fails that test is movable by definition.

options.text: Property of every description except land and buildings
options.explanation: Too narrow an exclusion. Benefits arising out of land, and things permanently fastened to what is attached to the earth, are also immovable.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Month and year
questions.stem: Under section 3 of the General Clauses Act 1897, the expressions 'month' and 'year' mean:

readLink.label: Read: Section 3 — the definitions that matter →

options.text: A period of thirty days and a period of three hundred and sixty-five days respectively
options.explanation: This is the error the definition exists to prevent. One month from 31 January 2027 ends on 28 February 2027; thirty days from the same date ends on 2 March 2027.

options.text: A calendar month, and the financial year commencing on the first day of April
options.explanation: 'Financial year' is separately defined in s. 3 and is a different expression. A bare 'year' is not the financial year.

options.text: A lunar month, and a period of twelve lunar months
options.explanation: The Act adopts a solar, not a lunar, reckoning.

options.text: A month and a year reckoned according to the British calendar
options.explanation: Correct. 'British calendar' means the Gregorian calendar, so a month runs to the corresponding day of the following month (or, where there is none, to the last day of that month) and a year to the corresponding day of the following year.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Person, imprisonment, offence and registered
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the section 3 definitions in the General Clauses Act 1897 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Good faith, person and property →

options.text: 'Imprisonment' means simple imprisonment only, rigorous imprisonment requiring express words in the penal provision
options.explanation: 'Imprisonment' means imprisonment of EITHER description as defined in the Indian Penal Code — simple or rigorous.

options.text: 'Person' includes any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not
options.explanation: Correct. Because the definition uses 'includes', a natural person remains a person; the extension brings in companies, and unincorporated bodies such as firms, clubs and associations, without the later Act having to say so.

options.text: 'Offence' means an act or omission which is morally wrongful, whether or not it is punishable by law
options.explanation: Punishability, not morality, is the test: an offence is any act or omission made punishable by any law for the time being in force.

options.text: 'Registered', with reference to a document, includes registration under the law of any country
options.explanation: The definition requires registration IN INDIA under the law for the time being in force for the registration of documents.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 5 · Commencement where the Act is silent
questions.stem: A Central Act contains no provision as to when it is to come into operation. Under section 5 of the General Clauses Act 1897 it comes into operation on the day:

readLink.label: Read: Section 5 — commencement of enactments →

options.text: On which it receives the assent of the President
options.explanation: Correct. Where a Central Act is not expressed to come into operation on a particular day, it commences on the day it receives the assent — of the President for an Act of Parliament.

options.text: On which it is passed by both Houses of Parliament
options.explanation: Passing is not commencement. An Act passed on one day may receive assent days or weeks later, and s. 5 fixes on the assent.

options.text: On which it is published in the Official Gazette
options.explanation: Publication is a matter of notice, not of commencement. Section 5 names the assent, not the publication.

options.text: Thirty days after it receives the assent of the President
options.explanation: There is no waiting period. Section 5 fixes the day of assent itself.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 5 · The first moment of the commencement day
questions.stem: Where an enactment is to come into operation on a particular day, it is construed, unless the contrary is expressed, as coming into operation:

readLink.label: Read: Section 5 — commencement of enactments →

options.text: From the hour at which the notification appointing that day is published
options.explanation: The hour of publication of the notification is immaterial. The Act operates for the whole of the appointed day.

options.text: From the beginning of office hours on that day, acts done earlier in the day being outside it
options.explanation: There is no office-hours rule. A transaction at 6.30 a.m. on the commencement day is caught.

options.text: Immediately on the expiration of the day preceding its commencement, that is, from the first moment of the commencement day
options.explanation: Correct. The construction is that the enactment begins to operate the instant the previous day ends, so the whole of the commencement day is within it. There is no part-day operation.

options.text: From the expiration of the commencement day, so that the whole of that day falls outside the enactment
options.explanation: This defers operation by a full day and reverses the rule.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 6 · What a repeal does not do
questions.stem: Which of the following does section 6 of the General Clauses Act 1897 expressly declare that a repeal shall NOT do, unless a different intention appears?

readLink.label: Read: Sections 6 to 8 — the effect of repeal →

options.text: Preserve a right acquired under the repealed enactment
options.explanation: Section 6(c) preserves exactly that — the repeal shall not AFFECT a right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the repealed enactment.

options.text: Preserve a penalty incurred for an offence committed against the repealed enactment
options.explanation: Section 6(d) preserves it: the repeal shall not affect any penalty, forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect of an offence committed against the repealed enactment.

options.text: Permit a legal proceeding in respect of a liability incurred under the repealed enactment to be continued
options.explanation: Section 6(e) and its concluding words permit exactly that — such a proceeding may be instituted, continued or enforced as if the repealing Act had not been passed.

options.text: Revive an earlier law which was not in force at the time the repeal took effect
options.explanation: Correct. Section 6(a) declares that the repeal shall not revive anything not in force or existing at the time the repeal takes effect. Revival is never automatic — section 7 requires express words.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 6 · Prosecution begun after the repeal
questions.stem: Ravindra committed an offence under a Central Act in April 2026. That Act was repealed in July 2026, and no prosecution had been launched by then. The repealing Act says nothing about pending or future proceedings. Under section 6 of the General Clauses Act 1897:

readLink.label: Read: Sections 6 to 8 — the effect of repeal →

options.text: No prosecution can now be launched, the offence-creating provision having ceased to exist
options.explanation: That is the very result s. 6 exists to prevent. The penalty incurred is saved by 6(d) and the proceeding by 6(e).

options.text: A prosecution may be instituted and continued, and the punishment imposed, as if the repealing Act had not been passed
options.explanation: Correct. The concluding words of s. 6 say that any such investigation, legal proceeding or remedy may be INSTITUTED, continued or enforced, and any such penalty may be imposed, as if the repealing Act had not been passed. Institution after the repeal is expressly permitted.

options.text: A prosecution may be continued only if it had already been instituted before the repeal took effect
options.explanation: This reads the word 'instituted' out of the section. The saving is not confined to proceedings already begun.

options.text: A prosecution may be launched only with the previous sanction of the Central Government
options.explanation: Section 6 imposes no sanction requirement; it simply preserves the position as if the repeal had not happened.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · ss. 6A and 7 · Amending Acts and revival
questions.stem: Which statement about sections 6A and 7 of the General Clauses Act 1897 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Sections 6 to 8 — the effect of repeal →

options.text: The repeal of an Act which had textually amended a principal Act does not, unless a different intention appears, affect the continuance of that amendment; and the revival of a repealed enactment requires express words
options.explanation: Correct. Section 6A keeps a textual amendment alive when the spent amending Act is repealed, and section 7 requires a later Central Act to state the purpose of revival expressly.

options.text: The repeal of an amending Act automatically restores the principal Act to the text it bore before the amendment, and revival of a repealed enactment may be implied
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong. Section 6A preserves the amendment, and section 7 excludes implied revival.

options.text: Section 6A operates only where the amendment was made by express omission, and the revival of a repealed enactment follows automatically on the repeal of the repealing Act
options.explanation: Section 6A covers amendment by express omission, insertion OR substitution, and revival is never automatic.

options.text: Section 6A applies only where the amending Act is repealed within five years, and section 7 requires the previous approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: Neither the five-year limit nor the approval requirement exists.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 8 · References to repealed enactments
questions.stem: Section 8 of the General Clauses Act 1897 operates where a Central Act:

readLink.label: Read: Sections 6 to 8 — the effect of repeal →

options.text: Repeals any provision of a former enactment, whether or not it re-enacts that provision
options.explanation: A bare repeal is not enough. Without a re-enactment there is nothing for the old reference to be read as pointing to.

options.text: Re-enacts a provision without repealing the earlier one, the two provisions then operating together
options.explanation: The section requires a repeal as well as a re-enactment; two provisions operating side by side raise a different question altogether.

options.text: Repeals and re-enacts, with or without modification, a provision of a former enactment, so that references to the repealed provision in any other enactment or in any instrument are construed as references to the re-enacted provision
options.explanation: Correct. Three examinable features: repeal AND re-enactment; the re-enactment may be with modification; and the rule reaches instruments — contracts, deeds and notifications — as well as other enactments.

options.text: Repeals and re-enacts a provision without any modification, any modification taking the case outside the section
options.explanation: The section says 'with or without modification' in terms. Modification does not defeat it.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 9 · From and to
questions.stem: In a Central Act the words 'from' and 'to' are used to mark out a period of time. Under section 9 of the General Clauses Act 1897:

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

options.text: Both the first and the last day of the period are included
options.explanation: That would make 'from' inclusive, which is precisely what s. 9 denies.

options.text: Both the first and the last day of the period are excluded
options.explanation: 'To' is expressly used for the purpose of INCLUDING the last day.

options.text: 'From' includes the first day and 'to' excludes the last day
options.explanation: This inverts the section exactly, and produces an answer two days out on a typical computation.

options.text: 'From' excludes the first day and 'to' includes the last day
options.explanation: Correct. Section 9 says it is sufficient to use 'from' to exclude the first in a series of days, and 'to' to include the last. The two words do opposite work, and both are examined.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 9 · Twenty-one days from a date
questions.stem: A Central Act allows an objection to be filed within 21 days from 5 March 2027. Applying section 9 of the General Clauses Act 1897, the last day for filing the objection is:
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 9 — 'from' excludes the first day

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

options.text: 25 March 2027
options.explanation: This counts 5 March itself as day one. Section 9 excludes the first day, so the count begins on 6 March and this answer is one day short.

options.text: 26 March 2027
options.explanation: Correct. 5 March is excluded, so day 1 is 6 March 2027 and day 21 is 26 March 2027 — that is, the trigger date plus 21 days.

options.text: 27 March 2027
options.explanation: One day too many: this excludes the first day and then also counts an extra day at the end, which section 9 does not require.

options.text: 5 April 2027
options.explanation: This reads '21 days' as if it were a calendar month. The Act says days, and days are counted as days.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 9 · Sixty days across a month end
questions.stem: A Central Act requires a return to be furnished within 60 days from 15 January 2027. Applying section 9 of the General Clauses Act 1897, the last day for furnishing the return is:
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 9 — 'from' excludes the first day

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

options.text: 16 March 2027
options.explanation: Correct. 15 January is excluded, so the count runs from 16 January. Sixteen days remain in January, February 2027 has 28 days (2027 is not a leap year), and the remaining 16 days carry the count to 16 March 2027.

options.text: 15 March 2027
options.explanation: This counts 15 January as day one, contrary to section 9, and lands one day short.

options.text: 17 March 2027
options.explanation: One day too many — the first day is excluded once, not twice.

options.text: 15 April 2027
options.explanation: This counts 90 days, not 60. Read the number in the stem before reaching for the calendar.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 9 · Counting a 'from … to' period
questions.stem: A scheme framed under a Central Act is expressed to operate from 10 June 2026 to 9 September 2026. Applying section 9 of the General Clauses Act 1897, the number of days for which the scheme operates is:
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 9 — 'from' excludes the first day, 'to' includes the last

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

options.text: 90 days
options.explanation: This excludes the last day as well as the first. The word 'to' is used precisely to INCLUDE the last day, so 9 September must be counted.

options.text: 92 days
options.explanation: This includes both ends. 'From' excludes 10 June, so that day cannot be counted.

options.text: 91 days
options.explanation: Correct. 10 June is excluded and 9 September is included: 20 days in June, 31 in July, 31 in August and 9 in September — 91 days in all.

options.text: 89 days
options.explanation: This drops a day at each end, excluding the last day twice over.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 10 · The closed-day rule
questions.stem: Section 10 of the General Clauses Act 1897 applies where an act or proceeding directed or allowed to be done in a court or office:

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

options.text: Falls due on a day on which the person required to do it is unable to attend for reasons beyond his control
options.explanation: The section looks at the closure of the court or office, not at the difficulties of the individual.

options.text: Cannot be completed because the court or office is closed on any day during the prescribed period
options.explanation: A closure in the middle of the period does nothing at all. Section 10 looks only at the LAST day.

options.text: Falls due on a day on which the court or office is closed, in which case the prescribed period is extended by the number of closed days
options.explanation: There is no day-for-day extension. The act must be done on the next day the court or office is open.

options.text: Falls due on a day, or has as the last day of the prescribed period a day, on which the court or office is closed — in which case doing the act on the next day afterwards on which the court or office is open is in due time
options.explanation: Correct. The relief is a single step to the next open day, and it is triggered only by closure on the appointed day or on the last day of the period.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · ss. 9 and 10 · A closed last day
questions.stem: A Central Act requires an objection to be lodged in the office of a Controller within 30 days from 2 February 2027. That office is closed on 4 and 5 March 2027 (declared holidays) and on 6 and 7 March 2027 (the weekend), and reopens on 8 March 2027. The objection is lodged in due time if it is lodged on:

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

options.text: 4 March 2027
options.explanation: This is the last day of the 30-day period computed under section 9, but the office is closed on that day. Section 10 carries the deadline forward.

options.text: 8 March 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Under section 9, 2 February is excluded and the 30th day is 4 March 2027 (26 days remain in a 28-day February, plus 4 days in March). The office is closed from 4 to 7 March, so under section 10 lodging on 8 March — the next day on which the office is open — is in due time.

options.text: 5 March 2027
options.explanation: The day after the last day, but the office is still closed. Section 10 moves the act to the next OPEN day, not to the next day.

options.text: 3 March 2027
options.explanation: This counts 2 February as day one, contrary to section 9, and produces a deadline one day early.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · ss. 9 and 10 · Appeal on the next open day
questions.stem: A Central Act requires an appeal to be preferred within 15 days from 20 August 2026 in the office of an authority which is closed on 4 September 2026 (a declared holiday) and on 5 and 6 September 2026 (the weekend), and reopens on 7 September 2026. The appeal is in time if it is preferred on:

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

options.text: 7 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 9 excludes 20 August, so the 15th day is 4 September 2026 (11 days remain in August plus 4 in September). That day and the two following days are closed, so section 10 permits the appeal to be preferred on 7 September, the next open day.

options.text: 4 September 2026
options.explanation: The last day computed under section 9 — but the office is closed on it, which is exactly the situation section 10 addresses.

options.text: 5 September 2026
options.explanation: The office is closed on 5 September too. The relief runs to the next day the office is OPEN.

options.text: 3 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts 20 August as day one, contrary to section 9.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 10 · The Limitation Act carve-out
questions.stem: Section 10 of the General Clauses Act 1897 does NOT apply to:
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 10 — proviso as to the Limitation Act

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

options.text: An act to be done in a public office under a rule made under a Central Act
options.explanation: Such an act is within the section — it covers acts directed or allowed to be done in a court or office under a Central Act or Regulation, and the subordinate legislation made under one.

options.text: An act to be done in a court, courts being governed only by their own rules
options.explanation: Courts are expressly named in the section. It speaks of an act or proceeding to be done or taken 'in any court or office'.

options.text: Any act or proceeding to which the Limitation Act applies
options.explanation: Correct. The section carries its own carve-out. The Limitation Act has its own closed-day provision, so the protection is not lost — but the provision to be cited is that Act, not section 10.

options.text: An act which falls due on a day on which the office is open for part of the day only
options.explanation: An office open for part of the day is not closed, so no question of the section arises. That is not the carve-out.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 27 · Deemed service by post
questions.stem: Under section 27 of the General Clauses Act 1897, service of a document by post is deemed to be effected by:

readLink.label: Read: Section 27 — service by post →

options.text: Posting a properly addressed letter by ordinary post, service being conclusive from the date of posting
options.explanation: Two errors: the section requires REGISTERED post, and the deemed time of service is when the letter would arrive in the ordinary course of post, not the date of posting — and it is rebuttable.

options.text: Properly addressing and posting the letter, pre-payment being immaterial, service being effected only on actual delivery
options.explanation: Pre-payment is one of the three requirements, and the section deems service without proof of actual delivery.

options.text: Properly addressing, pre-paying and posting the letter by registered post, service being irrebuttably deemed effected on the seventh day after posting
options.explanation: There is no fixed seven-day rule, and the deeming as to time is expressly displaced where the contrary is proved.

options.text: Properly addressing, pre-paying and posting by registered post a letter containing the document, service being deemed effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post, unless the contrary is proved
options.explanation: Correct. Three acts establish service — proper address, pre-payment and posting by registered post — and the TIME of service is fixed by the ordinary course of post, subject to proof to the contrary. The whole section also yields where a different intention appears in the Act.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 27 · Ordinary course of post
questions.stem: A Central Act requires an order to be sent by post. The Controller properly addresses, pre-pays and posts the order by registered post on 3 February 2027. Evidence establishes that a letter so posted on that route is delivered in the ordinary course of post on the fourth day after posting. Unless the contrary is proved, service is deemed to have been effected on:

readLink.label: Read: Section 27 — service by post →

options.text: 6 February 2027
options.explanation: This is the third day after posting. The evidence fixes the ordinary course of post at the fourth day.

options.text: 7 February 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Posting on 3 February plus four days brings the letter to the addressee on 7 February 2027, and section 27 deems service to have been effected at that time — unless the contrary is proved.

options.text: 3 February 2027
options.explanation: The date of posting is when the sender does the three acts required by the section; it is not the deemed time of service.

options.text: 10 February 2027
options.explanation: A week after posting. Section 27 supplies no fixed period — the deemed time follows the ordinary course of post proved in the case.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 27 · Service across a month end
questions.stem: A notice required by a Central Act to be given by post is properly addressed, pre-paid and posted by registered post on 27 February 2027. A letter so posted is delivered in the ordinary course of post on the fourth day after posting. Service is deemed to have been effected on:

readLink.label: Read: Section 27 — service by post →

options.text: 3 March 2027
options.explanation: Correct. February 2027 has 28 days (2027 is not a leap year), so the fourth day after 27 February is 28 February, then 1, 2 and 3 March — service is deemed effected on 3 March 2027, unless the contrary is proved.

options.text: 2 March 2027
options.explanation: This treats February 2027 as having 29 days. 2027 is not a leap year.

options.text: 27 February 2027
options.explanation: The date of posting, not the deemed time of service.

options.text: 4 March 2027
options.explanation: The fifth day after posting. The stem fixes the ordinary course of post at the fourth day.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 11 · Measurement of distance
questions.stem: For the purposes of a Central Act, and unless a different intention appears, a distance is measured:

readLink.label: Read: Distance, gender and double punishment →

options.text: Along the shortest route by which it may lawfully be travelled
options.explanation: The route actually available is irrelevant. A road winding for nine kilometres between two points five kilometres apart does not make the distance nine.

options.text: Along the actual route travelled, including any vertical elevation on the way
options.explanation: Neither the route nor the elevation counts. Section 11 requires a straight line on a horizontal plane.

options.text: In a straight line on a horizontal plane
options.explanation: Correct. The 'crow-flight' measure: the route travelled is ignored, and vertical elevation between the two points is ignored because the measurement is taken on a horizontal plane.

options.text: In a straight line, with the vertical elevation between the two points added to the result
options.explanation: Adding the elevation is precisely what the words 'on a horizontal plane' exclude.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 13 · Gender and number
questions.stem: Section 13 of the General Clauses Act 1897 provides that, in all Central Acts and Regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context:

readLink.label: Read: Distance, gender and double punishment →

options.text: Words importing the masculine gender include females, but words in the singular never include the plural
options.explanation: Both limbs are in the section. The number limb is not omitted.

options.text: Words in the singular include the plural, but the masculine gender must be expressly extended to females in each Act
options.explanation: No express extension is needed. The masculine is taken to include females by force of section 13 itself.

options.text: The masculine gender includes females only in penal provisions
options.explanation: There is no such confinement. The rule runs across all Central Acts and Regulations.

options.text: Words importing the masculine gender are taken to include females, and words in the singular include the plural and words in the plural include the singular
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs operate, and both are subject to the safety valve — anything repugnant in the subject or context displaces them.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 26 · Offence punishable under two enactments
questions.stem: An act constitutes an offence under two Central Acts. Under section 26 of the General Clauses Act 1897, the offender:

readLink.label: Read: Distance, gender and double punishment →

options.text: May be prosecuted only under the enactment which prescribes the higher punishment
options.explanation: The section leaves the choice of enactment open and says nothing about the severity of the punishment.

options.text: May be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be liable to be punished twice for the same offence
options.explanation: Correct. The section bars double PUNISHMENT, not double prosecution. The prosecuting agency chooses its enactment, and proceedings under one are not barred merely because another was available.

options.text: May be prosecuted only once, a prosecution under one enactment barring all proceedings under the other
options.explanation: This converts a bar on double punishment into a bar on double prosecution, which the section does not impose.

options.text: May himself elect the enactment under which he is to be prosecuted
options.explanation: The offender has no such election. The section confers no choice on him at all.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 14 · Powers exercisable from time to time
questions.stem: Where a Central Act confers a power, then, unless a different intention appears, that power:

readLink.label: Read: Powers and functionaries — ss. 14 to 24 →

options.text: May be exercised from time to time as occasion requires
options.explanation: Correct. A statutory power is not spent on first use; section 14 makes it a continuing power unless the Act shows otherwise.

options.text: Is exhausted once it has been validly exercised
options.explanation: This is the very proposition section 14 was enacted to negative.

options.text: May be exercised only once in each financial year
options.explanation: No periodicity is imposed. The power is exercisable as occasion requires.

options.text: May be exercised only with the previous sanction of the Central Government
options.explanation: Section 14 adds no sanction requirement; it addresses only how often the power may be used.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 15 · Appointment by name or by office
questions.stem: Where a Central Act confers a power to appoint a person to fill an office or to execute a function, then, unless it is otherwise expressly provided, the appointment:

readLink.label: Read: Powers and functionaries — ss. 14 to 24 →

options.text: Must be made by name, an appointment by virtue of office requiring express words
options.explanation: The section permits both. No express words are needed for an ex officio appointment.

options.text: Must be made by virtue of office, an appointment by name being void
options.explanation: The reverse error. An appointment by name is perfectly valid.

options.text: May be made either by name or by virtue of office
options.explanation: Correct. Section 15 allows the appointing authority to name an individual, or to attach the office or function to the holder of another office for the time being.

options.text: May be made by name only where the appointee holds no other statutory office
options.explanation: No such condition exists in the section.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 16 · Power to appoint includes power to dismiss
questions.stem: Aakash was appointed to a statutory office by Authority X in exercise of a power of appointment conferred by a Central Act. That power now vests, for the time being, in Authority Y. Under section 16 of the General Clauses Act 1897:

readLink.label: Read: Powers and functionaries — ss. 14 to 24 →

options.text: Only Authority X may suspend or dismiss Aakash, being the authority which in fact appointed him
options.explanation: Section 16 attaches the power to the authority having the appointing power FOR THE TIME BEING, not to whoever happened to make the appointment.

options.text: Neither authority may dismiss Aakash unless the Act confers an express power of dismissal
options.explanation: No express power is needed. The power to suspend or dismiss is implied by section 16 from the power to appoint.

options.text: Authority Y may suspend Aakash but may not dismiss him, dismissal requiring express words
options.explanation: The section names both suspension and dismissal; there is no half measure.

options.text: Authority Y, having for the time being the power to make the appointment, may suspend or dismiss Aakash notwithstanding that he was appointed by Authority X
options.explanation: Correct. Section 16 expressly extends to a person appointed 'whether by itself or any other authority' in exercise of that power, and it operates unless a different intention appears.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · ss. 17 to 19 · Functionaries, successors and subordinates
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about sections 17 to 19 of the General Clauses Act 1897 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Powers and functionaries — ss. 14 to 24 →

options.text: Each of the three situations they address requires express words in the later Act before the law can be applied
options.explanation: The sections exist to make express words unnecessary. Each says that a shorter form of words 'shall be sufficient'.

options.text: To apply a law to whoever for the time being executes the functions of an office it is sufficient to mention the official title; to relate a law to successors it is sufficient to express its relation to the functionaries or bodies themselves; and to apply a law relating to a superior to deputies lawfully performing his duties in his place it is sufficient to prescribe the duty of the superior
options.explanation: Correct. Sections 17, 18 and 19 in that order — official title, successors, and deputies or subordinates lawfully performing the superior's duties.

options.text: A law relating to the chief or superior of an office can never be applied to a deputy performing his duties
options.explanation: Section 19 says the opposite: prescribing the duty of the superior suffices to reach a deputy lawfully performing those duties in his place.

options.text: A law is related to the successors of a functionary only if the later Act names those successors individually
options.explanation: Section 18 makes it sufficient to express the law's relation to the functionaries or bodies; naming successors is unnecessary.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 21 · Power to add to, amend, vary or rescind
questions.stem: A power conferred by a Central Act to issue notifications, orders, rules or bye-laws includes a power to add to, amend, vary or rescind them. That power to vary or rescind is exercisable:

readLink.label: Read: Powers and functionaries — ss. 14 to 24 →

options.text: In the like manner and subject to the like sanction and conditions (if any) as attached to the original exercise of the power
options.explanation: Correct. Section 21 is about symmetry: if consultation, previous publication or another authority's approval was required to issue the instrument, the same steps are required to vary or rescind it.

options.text: At any time and in any manner the authority thinks fit, the conditions attaching only to the original issue
options.explanation: This drops the qualifying words of the section, which are the point of the whole provision.

options.text: Only with the previous approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: No such approval is imposed. The conditions are those which governed the original exercise of the power.

options.text: Only where the parent Act expressly confers a power of amendment or rescission
options.explanation: The power is implied by section 21 precisely so that express words are unnecessary.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 22 · Rules made between passing and commencement
questions.stem: A Central Act is passed on 12 January 2027 but is to come into force on 1 May 2027. It confers a power to make rules with respect to the manner in which things are to be done under it. Rules are made on 20 March 2027. Under section 22 of the General Clauses Act 1897, those rules:

readLink.label: Read: Powers and functionaries — ss. 14 to 24 →

options.text: Are void, the rule-making power not having come into existence before the Act commenced
options.explanation: Section 22 exists to prevent that result. The power may be exercised at any time after the Act is passed.

options.text: Are validly made and take effect from 20 March 2027, the date on which they were made
options.explanation: They are validly made, but section 22 postpones their effect. Nothing made under the Act can operate before the Act itself does.

options.text: Are validly made, the power being exercisable at any time after the passing of the Act, but do not take effect until the Act commences on 1 May 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Section 22 separates making from taking effect: rules, bye-laws and the specified orders may be made in the interval, so that the machinery is ready, but they operate only from commencement.

options.text: Are validly made and take effect from 12 January 2027, the date on which the Act was passed
options.explanation: Backdating the rules to the date of passing would give the Act operation before its own commencement.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · Scheme · Object and application of the General Clauses Act
questions.stem: Explain the object of the General Clauses Act 1897 and state the enactments to which it applies. In what circumstances does the Act not govern the construction of a provision? (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Object 1 — economy of drafting: the Act defines commonly used expressions once, in s. 3, so that Parliament need not repeat those definitions in every Central Act it passes; the definitions are borrowed by every later Central Act

Object 2 — uniformity and certainty: the same expression bears the same meaning across the statute book, so that a court does not give an expression one sense in one Central Act and a different sense in another unless the legislature says so

Object 3 — supply of defaults where the later Act is silent: commencement (s. 5), the effect of a repeal (s. 6), the computation of time (ss. 9 and 10), the exercise of powers (s. 14) and service by post (s. 27) all operate without the later Act saying a word

Application: the Act governs Central Acts and Regulations, and — through the extending provisions — the rules, regulations and bye-laws made under Central Acts; a State Act is governed by the General Clauses Act of that State, not by this Act

When it does not govern: (i) where the enactment being construed supplies its own definition of the expression; (ii) where there is something repugnant in the subject or context; (iii) where a different intention appears from the later enactment, the words in which most operative sections are expressed; and (iv) where the legislation is State legislation
skeleton.citation: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 3 opening words; ss. 6, 8, 11, 14, 16 and 27 ('unless a different intention appears')

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 3 · Definitions with illustrations
questions.stem: Define the following expressions as they are defined in the General Clauses Act 1897, illustrating each: (i) good faith, (ii) immovable property, (iii) movable property, (iv) person, (v) month and year, and (vi) affidavit, oath and swear. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Good faith: a thing is deemed to be done in good faith where it is in fact done honestly, whether it is done negligently or not — a test of subjective honesty. Contrast s. 52 of the Indian Penal Code, under which nothing is done in good faith which is done without due care and attention; where the enactment supplies its own definition, that definition governs. Illustration: a clerk who posts a notice to an address he honestly believes current, without checking the register, acts in good faith under this Act though negligently
skeleton.citation: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 3 — 'good faith'; Indian Penal Code, s. 52 (contrast)

skeleton.point: Immovable property: includes (a) land, (b) benefits to arise out of land, and (c) things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth. Illustration: a right to draw water from a well on another's land, and an overhead tank bolted to a plinth cast into the ground, are both immovable property

Movable property: property of every description except immovable property — a residual definition, so the working method is to test immovability first. Illustration: a diesel generator standing loose on a factory floor is movable property

Person: includes any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not; because the definition is inclusive, a natural person remains a person. Illustration: a provision penalising 'any person' who fails to file a return reaches an unregistered association as well as an individual

Month and year: a month and a year reckoned according to the British (Gregorian) calendar, and not a period of thirty days or of 365 days. Illustration: one month from 31 January 2027 expires on 28 February 2027, whereas thirty days from that date expires on 2 March 2027

Affidavit, oath and swear: 'affidavit' includes affirmation and declaration in the case of persons by law allowed to affirm or declare instead of swearing; 'oath' includes affirmation and declaration in the same class of case; and 'swear' includes affirming and declaring in that class of case

questions.topic: Ch 13 · ss. 6, 6A and 7 · Effect of repeal
questions.stem: State the effect of the repeal of an enactment under section 6 of the General Clauses Act 1897. Explain also the effect of the repeal of an Act which had textually amended a principal Act, and the requirement for reviving a repealed enactment. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: The governing qualification: the savings in s. 6 operate where a Central Act or Regulation repeals an enactment, and they operate only 'unless a different intention appears' from the repealing enactment; the savings are defaults, not guarantees
skeleton.citation: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 6 — opening words

skeleton.point: Clause (a): the repeal shall not revive anything not in force or existing at the time at which the repeal takes effect — an earlier law which the repealed enactment had itself displaced does not come back to life

Clause (b): the repeal shall not affect the previous operation of the enactment so repealed, or anything duly done or suffered thereunder — assessments made, licences granted and acts already done stand
Clause (c): the repeal shall not affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the repealed enactment
Clause (d): the repeal shall not affect any penalty, forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against the repealed enactment

Clause (e) and the concluding words: the repeal shall not affect any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy in respect of any such right, privilege, obligation, liability, penalty, forfeiture or punishment; and any such investigation, legal proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced, and any such penalty, forfeiture or punishment may be imposed, as if the repealing Act had not been passed — so a prosecution may be BEGUN after the repeal for an offence committed before it
skeleton.citation: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 6(e) and concluding words

skeleton.point: Section 6A: where a later Central Act repeals an enactment by which the text of a Central Act or Regulation was amended by express omission, insertion or substitution, then, unless a different intention appears, the repeal does not affect the continuance of that amendment — repealing the spent amending Act does not restore the earlier text of the principal Act

Section 7: to revive, wholly or partially, an enactment wholly or partially repealed, a later Central Act or Regulation must expressly state that purpose; there is no implied revival, which is the counterpart of s. 6(a)

questions.topic: Ch 13 · ss. 9 and 10 · Computation of time
questions.stem: Explain, with an illustration, how a period of time is computed under sections 9 and 10 of the General Clauses Act 1897, and state the limits of section 10. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 9: in a Central Act it is sufficient, for the purpose of EXCLUDING the first in a series of days or any other period of time, to use the word 'from'; and, for the purpose of INCLUDING the last, to use the word 'to'. The two words therefore do opposite work — 'from' pushes the start forward by a day, 'to' keeps the whole of the last day within the period

Illustration on s. 9: where an Act allows an objection to be filed within 21 days from 5 March 2027, 5 March is excluded, the count begins on 6 March, and the last day is 26 March 2027. Counting 5 March as day one and answering 25 March is the standard error
skeleton.citation: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 9 — worked application

skeleton.point: Section 10: where a Central Act or Regulation directs or allows any act or proceeding to be done or taken in any court or office on a certain day or within a prescribed period, and the court or office is closed on that day or on the last day of the period, the act or proceeding is considered as done or taken in due time if it is done or taken on the next day afterwards on which the court or office is open

Limits of s. 10 (i): the act must be one to be done in a COURT or OFFICE, and it is the closure of that court or office on the LAST day (or on the appointed day) that matters; a closure on an intermediate day within the period has no effect at all, and the relief carries the act to the next OPEN day, not merely to the next day

Limits of s. 10 (ii): the section does not apply to any act or proceeding to which the Limitation Act applies — such acts are protected by that Act's own provision, so the correct provision to cite in a limitation matter is the Limitation Act and not s. 10

questions.topic: Ch 13 · s. 27 · Meaning of service by post
questions.stem: Explain the meaning of 'service by post' under section 27 of the General Clauses Act 1897. When is such service deemed to be effected, and to what extent may the deeming be displaced? (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Scope: the section applies where a Central Act or Regulation authorises or requires a document to be served by post, and it applies whether the enactment uses the expression 'serve', 'give', 'send' or any other expression; the whole section yields where a different intention appears

The three requirements for deemed service: (i) properly ADDRESSING a letter containing the document, (ii) PRE-PAYING it, and (iii) POSTING it BY REGISTERED POST. All three must be satisfied; a letter sent by ordinary post, or a registered letter bearing a wrong address, falls outside the section and the sender must prove actual receipt

The deemed time of service: service is deemed to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post — not on the date of posting, and not on proof of actual delivery

Displacement of the deeming: the time limb operates 'unless the contrary is proved', so the addressee may show that the letter never arrived or arrived later, and the sender may show earlier delivery; refusal to accept a properly tendered registered letter does not assist the addressee
skeleton.citation: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 27 — 'unless the contrary is proved'

questions.topic: Ch 13 · ss. 14 to 24 · Powers, functionaries and subordinate legislation
questions.stem: State the rules laid down by the General Clauses Act 1897 with respect to the exercise of statutory powers and the persons who exercise them, dealing with sections 14, 15, 16, 17 to 19, 21, 22 and 23. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 14: where a Central Act or Regulation confers a power, then, unless a different intention appears, the power may be exercised from time to time as occasion requires — a statutory power is not exhausted by its first valid exercise

Section 15: where a power to appoint a person to fill an office or execute a function is conferred, then, unless it is otherwise expressly provided, the appointment may be made either by name or by virtue of office

Section 16: where a power to make an appointment is conferred, the authority having for the time being the power to make the appointment also has the power to suspend or dismiss any person appointed in exercise of that power, whether appointed by itself or by any other authority — unless a different intention appears

Sections 17 to 19: it is sufficient to mention the official title of the officer presently executing the functions, or of the officer by whom they are commonly executed, to apply a law to every person for the time being executing them (s. 17); it is sufficient to express a law's relation to functionaries or bodies to relate it to their successors (s. 18); and it is sufficient to prescribe the duty of the superior to apply a law relating to the chief or superior of an office to deputies or subordinates lawfully performing his duties in his place (s. 19)

Section 21: a power to issue notifications, orders, rules or bye-laws includes a power to add to, amend, vary or rescind them — but that power is exercisable in the like manner and subject to the like sanction and conditions (if any) as governed the original exercise, so any required consultation, previous publication or approval must be repeated

Section 22: where a Central Act or Regulation is not to come into force immediately on its passing, a power under it to make rules or bye-laws, or to issue the orders specified in the section, may be exercised at any time after the passing of the Act; but such rules, bye-laws or orders do not take effect until the Act commences

Section 23: where a rule-making power is given subject to previous publication — publish a draft for the information of persons likely to be affected, in the manner the authority deems sufficient or as prescribed; publish with it a notice specifying a date on or after which the draft will be taken into consideration; consider objections and suggestions received before that date; and publication of the rule in the Official Gazette as having been made after previous publication is conclusive proof that it was duly made

questions.topic: Ch 13 · Case: the section 3 definitions applied to a notice
questions.case: A Central Act empowers a Collector to require any 'person' in occupation of land to remove an unauthorised structure, and requires the requisition to be 'sent' to that person. The land at Meghdoot Enclave is occupied by the Meghdoot Allottees Forum, an unregistered association of forty allottees which has never been incorporated or registered under any law. On 24 December 2026 the Collector's office properly addresses, pre-pays and posts the requisition to the Forum by registered post; a letter so posted on that route is delivered in the ordinary course of post on the fifth day after posting. The clerk who addressed the letter used the address entered in the Collector's register, which he honestly believed to be current but which he had not verified for two years. The land carries a well from which the Forum is entitled to draw water for thirty years, an overhead tank permanently fastened to a concrete plinth cast into the ground, and a portable diesel generator standing on the floor of a shed. Two of the forty allottees are unable to write and affix their thumb impressions to the Forum's reply.

readLink.label: Read: Section 3 — the definitions that matter →

questions.stem: Is the Meghdoot Allottees Forum a 'person' within the meaning of the Act, so that a requisition may be addressed to it?

options.text: Yes — 'person' includes any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not, so an unregistered association is a person
options.explanation: Correct. The definition is inclusive and expressly covers a body of individuals whether incorporated or not; no registration or incorporation is required before the Forum can be a 'person'.

options.text: No — only a natural person or an incorporated company can be a 'person' under the Act
options.explanation: The definition expressly extends beyond natural persons and beyond incorporated bodies.

options.text: Yes, but only if the Forum first registers itself under some law for the time being in force
options.explanation: Registration is irrelevant. The words 'whether incorporated or not' put the matter beyond argument.

options.text: No — an association can be a 'person' only where the Central Act in question says so expressly
options.explanation: The point of the definition is that express words in the later Act are unnecessary.

questions.stem: Unless the contrary is proved, on what date is the requisition deemed to have been served on the Forum?

options.text: 24 December 2026
options.explanation: That is the date of posting — the date on which the sender performed the three acts the section requires. It is not the deemed time of service.

options.text: 28 December 2026
options.explanation: The fourth day after posting. The stem fixes the ordinary course of post at the fifth day.

options.text: 29 December 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Posting on 24 December plus five days in the ordinary course of post brings delivery to 29 December 2026, and section 27 deems service effected at that time unless the contrary is proved.

options.text: 31 December 2026
options.explanation: A week after posting. Section 27 supplies no fixed period; it follows the ordinary course of post proved in the case.

questions.stem: Applying the definitions in section 3 of the General Clauses Act 1897, which of the three items on the land is movable property?
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 3 — 'immovable property' and 'movable property'

options.text: The right to draw water from the well for thirty years
options.explanation: A right to draw water is a benefit to arise out of land, which the definition of immovable property expressly includes.

options.text: The overhead tank fastened to the concrete plinth
options.explanation: It is permanently fastened to something attached to the earth, and so falls in the third limb of the immovable-property definition.

options.text: The right to draw water and the overhead tank, both being severable from the land
options.explanation: Severability is not the test in this Act. Both items fall within the express limbs of the immovable-property definition.

options.text: The portable diesel generator standing on the floor of the shed
options.explanation: Correct. It is neither land, nor a benefit arising out of land, nor attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything so attached. Failing all three limbs, it is movable property under the residual definition.

questions.stem: As to the clerk's conduct and the thumb impressions, which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 3 — 'good faith' and 'sign'

options.text: The clerk did not act in good faith, because he failed to take due care; and the thumb impressions are not a valid signature
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: due care is not required by this Act's definition of good faith, and 'sign' includes 'mark' for a person unable to write.

options.text: The clerk acted in good faith, honesty being the test under this Act notwithstanding negligence; and the thumb impressions are a valid signing, 'sign' including 'mark' with reference to a person unable to write his name
options.explanation: Correct. Good faith under the General Clauses Act is honesty 'whether negligently or not', and the definition of 'sign' expressly includes a mark where the person concerned is unable to write his name.

options.text: The clerk acted in good faith, but the thumb impressions are ineffective because the definition of 'sign' requires a written signature in every case
options.explanation: The definition of 'sign' extends to a mark precisely for a person unable to write.

options.text: The clerk did not act in good faith, but the thumb impressions are valid because any mark is a signature under the Act
options.explanation: The first half applies the Penal Code's due-care standard, which does not govern here; and the extension of 'sign' to a mark is confined to a person unable to write his name.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · Case: repeal, re-enactment and what survives
questions.case: The (fictitious) Central Seed Certification Act 1998 made the sale of uncertified seed an offence and empowered the Government to notify certification standards. The Central Seed Certification Act 2026, brought into force on 1 August 2026, repeals the 1998 Act and re-enacts the offence provision, with modification, as its section 21. The 2026 Act also repeals the Central Seed Certification (Amendment) Act 2014, which had substituted a new definition of 'seed' in the text of the 1998 Act. Naveen sold uncertified seed on 12 May 2026; no prosecution had been instituted by 1 August 2026. A supply contract of 2009 between two parties refers to 'section 17 of the Central Seed Certification Act 1998'. A standards notification issued in 2019 under the 1998 Act is in force and is not inconsistent with the provisions re-enacted by the 2026 Act. The 2026 Act says nothing about pending or future proceedings and nothing about reviving the law which preceded the 1998 Act.

readLink.label: Read: Sections 6 to 8 — the effect of repeal →

questions.stem: What is the position as to the prosecution of Naveen for the sale on 12 May 2026?

options.text: A prosecution may be instituted after 1 August 2026 and carried to conviction and punishment, as if the repealing Act had not been passed
options.explanation: Correct. Section 6(d) saves the penalty incurred for an offence committed against the repealed enactment and section 6(e), with the concluding words of the section, permits the proceeding to be INSTITUTED, continued or enforced as if the repealing Act had not been passed.

options.text: No prosecution is now possible, the offence-creating provision of the 1998 Act having been repealed before any proceeding began
options.explanation: That is the result section 6 was enacted to prevent, and the saving is not limited to proceedings already begun.

options.text: Naveen may be prosecuted only under section 21 of the 2026 Act, which re-enacts the offence
options.explanation: The 2026 Act cannot be applied to conduct which preceded its commencement. The prosecution proceeds on the repealed provision, saved by section 6.

options.text: A prosecution is possible only if the 2026 Act expressly saves pending and future proceedings
options.explanation: No express saving is needed. Section 6 supplies it unless a different intention appears, and here the 2026 Act says nothing.

questions.stem: How is the reference in the 2009 supply contract to 'section 17 of the Central Seed Certification Act 1998' to be construed?

options.text: The reference is meaningless, section 8 applying only to references contained in other enactments and not to contracts
options.explanation: Section 8 expressly reaches a reference 'in any instrument', which includes a contract.

options.text: The reference stands as a reference to the 1998 Act, which continues in force between the contracting parties
options.explanation: A repealed Act does not survive between contracting parties. Section 8 redirects the reference instead.

options.text: The reference fails because the re-enactment was made with modification, which takes the case outside section 8
options.explanation: Section 8 applies where the provision is repealed and re-enacted 'with or without modification'.

options.text: The reference is construed as a reference to the corresponding provision re-enacted by the 2026 Act, unless a different intention appears
options.explanation: Correct. Section 8 applies where a provision is repealed AND re-enacted, with or without modification, and it redirects references in other enactments and in instruments alike.

questions.stem: What is the position of the 2019 standards notification, and of the law which preceded the 1998 Act?

options.text: The notification lapsed on 1 August 2026, and the pre-1998 law revived automatically on the repeal of the 1998 Act
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: section 24 continues the notification, and section 6(a) prevents any revival.

options.text: The notification continues in force so far as it is not inconsistent with the re-enacted provisions and is deemed issued under them until superseded; and the pre-1998 law is not revived
options.explanation: Correct. Section 24 preserves appointments, notifications, orders, schemes, rules, forms and bye-laws across a repeal and re-enactment, and sections 6(a) and 7 exclude any revival that is not expressly enacted.

options.text: The notification continues in force only if the 2026 Act expressly says so, and the pre-1998 law is not revived
options.explanation: The second half is right but the first is not: section 24 operates unless it is otherwise expressly provided, so silence preserves the notification.

options.text: The notification continues in force, and the pre-1998 law revives to the extent that the 2026 Act does not cover the same ground
options.explanation: There is no partial or gap-filling revival. Revival requires express words under section 7.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the repeal of the Central Seed Certification (Amendment) Act 2014, which had substituted a new definition of 'seed' in the 1998 Act?

options.text: The substituted definition ceases to have effect and the definition as it stood before 2014 is restored
options.explanation: That is exactly what section 6A prevents. A spent amending Act may be repealed without unpicking the amendment it made.

options.text: The repeal of the amending Act has no effect at all, because an amending Act cannot be repealed once its text has been absorbed
options.explanation: An amending Act can certainly be repealed; the point of section 6A is that the repeal does not disturb the amendment.

options.text: Unless a different intention appears, the repeal does not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the 2014 Act and in operation at the time of the repeal
options.explanation: Correct. Section 6A saves the continuance of a textual amendment made by express omission, insertion or substitution when the amending enactment is itself repealed.

options.text: The substituted definition continues only if the 2026 Act expressly preserves it
options.explanation: No express preservation is needed. Section 6A operates unless a different intention appears.

questions.topic: Ch 13 · Case: a filing deadline, a closed office and the Limitation Act
questions.case: A Central Act requires an aggrieved dealer to file a revision petition in the office of the Commissioner within forty-five days from the date of the order sought to be revised. The order against Kalinga Traders is dated 18 November 2026. The office of the Commissioner was closed on 25 December 2026, a declared holiday, and is closed on Saturday 2 January 2027 and Sunday 3 January 2027, reopening on Monday 4 January 2027. The revision is not a proceeding to which the Limitation Act 1963 applies.

readLink.label: Read: Sections 9 and 10 — computation of time →

questions.stem: Applying section 9 of the General Clauses Act 1897, the last day of the forty-five day period is:

options.text: 1 January 2027
options.explanation: This counts 18 November itself as day one. Section 9 excludes the first day, so this answer is one day short.

options.text: 2 January 2027
options.explanation: Correct. 18 November is excluded, so the count runs from 19 November: 12 days remain in November and 31 days in December, making 43, and the remaining two days carry the period to 2 January 2027.

options.text: 3 January 2027
options.explanation: One day too many — the first day is excluded once, not twice.

options.text: 18 December 2026
options.explanation: This reads forty-five days as if it were one calendar month. The Act speaks of days.

questions.stem: Applying section 10 of the General Clauses Act 1897, the revision petition is filed in due time if it is filed on:

options.text: 2 January 2027
options.explanation: That is the last day of the period, but the office is closed on it — which is precisely the situation section 10 addresses.

options.text: 3 January 2027
options.explanation: The next day after the last day, but the office is closed on 3 January too. Section 10 carries the act to the next OPEN day.

options.text: 4 January 2027
options.explanation: Correct. The last day, 2 January 2027, and the following day are both days on which the office is closed, so filing on 4 January 2027 — the next day on which the office is open — is in due time.

options.text: 1 January 2027
options.explanation: This treats 1 January as the last day, which is a section 9 miscount, and in any event ignores section 10 altogether.

questions.stem: What effect does the closure of the office on 25 December 2026 have on the computation?
questions.sourceRef: General Clauses Act 1897, s. 10 — closure of the last day only

options.text: None — section 10 is concerned only with closure on the appointed day or on the last day of the prescribed period, and a closure on an intermediate day does not extend the period
options.explanation: Correct. A holiday in the middle of the period is irrelevant; the period is not extended day for day, and only the closure of the last day attracts the section.

options.text: The period is extended by one day, because the office was closed for one day during it
options.explanation: There is no day-for-day extension in section 10.

options.text: The period is suspended from 25 December 2026 and begins to run again on the next open day
options.explanation: Section 10 contains no provision for suspending a running period.

options.text: The period is computed afresh from 26 December 2026
options.explanation: Nothing in section 9 or section 10 restarts a period because of a mid-period holiday.

questions.stem: Suppose instead that the revision were a proceeding to which the Limitation Act 1963 applies. The position would then be that:

options.text: Section 10 would still apply, the Limitation Act operating only in respect of suits
options.explanation: The carve-out in section 10 is not confined to suits; it excludes any act or proceeding to which the Limitation Act applies.

options.text: Neither section 10 nor any other provision would save a filing made after the last day
options.explanation: That is not so — the Limitation Act contains its own provision for a closed last day.

options.text: Section 10 would apply, but only after the remedies under the Limitation Act had been exhausted
options.explanation: There is no such sequencing. The two provisions do not operate one after the other.

options.text: Section 10 would not apply, because it does not extend to any act or proceeding to which the Limitation Act applies; the corresponding provision of that Act would govern instead
options.explanation: Correct. The result may well be the same, but the provision to be cited is the Limitation Act, not section 10 of the General Clauses Act.
